title: How This Year’s Black Friday Deals Explain the Tumultuous State of Streaming
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All November 27, 2026 10:35am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Seth Rogen in 'The Studio' Apple TV+ The streaming business is in flux, and Black Friday deals can help explain it. It’s not hyperbole: Netflix stock has been cut in half from its all-time high. Bundles are proliferating. And Skydance CEO David Ellison has made it clear that a merger of HBO Max and Paramount+ is a question of when, not if. Black Friday streaming deals are an annual tradition at this point, but given the state of the business, they can also shed light on how the entertainment giants behind them are thinking about the future of their products. Related Stories Lifestyle Black Friday Streaming Deals 2026: Disney+, Hulu, Apple TV and More Lifestyle Fubo Plans Now Include Free Disney+, Hulu, ESPN Unlimited and Fox One Netflix, for example, is the lone streamer not offering a Black Friday deal (at least as of writing). In fact, it has never offered a discount, underscoring its place in the streaming ecosystem as the unambiguous market leader: There’s no need to entice subscribers with a discount when you already have the market hooked. HBO Max and Paramount+ are offering very different types of deals, even as their parent company Skydance, is actively preparing for a discount bundle set for early next year, and with a full merger of the services following later on HBO Max is offering an aggressive 50 percent discount on its ad-supported tier, charging $5.49 per month for a full year. Paramount+, meanwhile, is offering both its premium and standard plans for $2.99 per month, albeit only for the first two months. With the bundle imminent and a merger coming (expect Paramount+’s tech stack to win out over HBO Max’s), the Black Friday deals are a last gasp before what is expected to be an aggressive discount campaign early next year. The biggest new streamer to launch in the last year, Fox One, is offering a steep 75 percent discount, $5 for the first month, before it reverts back to $20 in month two. Peacock, meanwhile, is offering generous discounts on both its select and premium plans, selling them for $2.99 and $8.99 per month for the first three months. The Paramount+, Fox One and Peacock deals are, conspicuously, time-limited, and that timing coincides with the heart of the NFL season. Subscribers will get hooked right as the NFL playoffs begin, with NBC, CBS and Fox (and their respective streamers) all holding those rights. Disney, which has been leaning into bundles, is offering a year of Disney+ and Hulu for $5 per month, hoping to get viewers hooked on its two entertainment platforms (ESPN is the other) ahead of a full sunset of the Hulu standalone app (it is expected to continue as a standalone service within Disney+). Apple TV, which is still trying to gain the scale that many of the other services already have, is offering an aggressive discount of over 50 percent, selling six months of the services for $6.99 per month, down from its typical price of $14.99 per month. And niche streamers are being more aggressive: Look at Starz, which is offering an astonishing deal: $11.99 for 12 months, putting the price at under $1 per month when buying the annual plan (a more modest discount is available on monthly plans), underscoring how it needs to gain scale, and fast. Crunchyroll, Sony’s anime-focused streamer, is also offering discounts of over 50 percent for six months, ranging from $3.99 for its base tier to $8.99 for its ultimate tier. Streaming is in a new phase, where consolidation and bundles are the norm, and the status quo of today won’t be so in a year. It’s a world where creative discounting may be required, even if the long-term strategy prefers profits over subscriber progress. And it’s a world where Netflix, the king of the crop, still feels as though it has no need to offer discounts of any sort. After all, when you have won the subscription streaming war, it’s better to keep those margins intact. THR

title: Doha Winners: ‘A Girl Unknown’ & ‘Concrete Land’ Scoop Top Prizes
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Michel Hazanavicius To Present Exclusive Footage Of ‘The Third Hand’ In AI Case Study At Les Arcs Warwick Thornton, Teona Strugar Mitevska & Myroslav Slaboshpytskiy Set For Rotterdam’s Cinemart Gérard Depardieu Rape Case Sent To Trial In Criminal Court After Actor Loses Appeal View All November 27, 2026 10:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A Girl Unknown Cannes Film Festival Chinese director Zou Jing’s A Girl Unknown won the top $75,000 Best Narrative prize at the Doha Film Festival as the second edition of its revamped format came to a close on Friday evening. The China-set first feature follows the fate of a young girl who is found abandoned as a baby in a rubbish bin and then grows up from babyhood through to adolescence with three sets of different guardians and circumstances. The film world premiered in Cannes Critics’ Week earlier this year where it won the Fipresci Prize. The picture was acquired for the U.S. by Greenwich Entertainment which is planning an early 2027 tour and release. Related Stories News International Insider: Doha Days; Tricky Week For BAFTA; 'Remarried Empress' Interview News Todd Boehly Dissects How Daniel Katz's Trading Desk Acumen Fed Into A24 Success: "Very Few Entertainment People Understand Math" Rafael Manuel won Best Artistic Achievement in Narrative for Filipiñana about a 17-year-old girl who discovers a rotten side to the posh countryclub where she works on the golf course. The film world premiered in Sundance, where it won the World Cinema Special Jury Award. The film is the Philippines’ entry for the 99th Academy Awards. Watch on Deadline Best Actress was awarded posthumously to Josette Kwanya for her performance in her son Auguste Bernard Kouemo’s House of the Wind as an elderly Cameroonian woman waiting for her children to return home after they left for Europe in search of fresh life opportunities. The film won Venice’s Lion of the Future for a Debut Film when it premiered there in its Orizzonti sidebar in September. This year’s jury was presided over by Japanese director Naomi Kawase, who was joined by by Oscar-winning documentarian Gianfranco Rosi, rising actor Adam Bessa, Tunisian producer Dora Bouchoucha and Palestinian director Kamal Aljafari. In further prizes, Best Documentary went to Asmahan Bkerat ’ s Concrete Land about a Bedouin family struggling to preserve their traditional way of life in tents, as well as the Fipresci prize, which is being awarded at the festival for the first time this year. In other documentary prizes, Tala Hadid’s Bardi won the Best Artistic Achievement for Documentary. Fatma Hassan Alremaihi, Festival Director and CEO of Doha Film Institute said the 2026 Doha Film Festival tapped into her institute’s belief in “the power of stories to transcend borders, challenge perspectives and bring the experiences of people and communities into the global conversation.” “At Doha Film Institute, we believe that important voices deserve to be seen, heard and recognised. Doha Film Festival exists to provide that platform, bringing together filmmakers and audiences from across the world, championing bold and independent storytelling, and creating space for stories that might otherwise go untold,” she said. “The films we honour tonight remind us that cinema is not simply a reflection of the world we live in; it is a force that can shape how we understand it, connect with one another and imagine a more empathetic future.” The full list of 2026 winners Special Mention: 9 Temples to Heaven by Sompot Chidgasornpongse Best Performance: Josette Kwanya from House of the Wind, directed by Auguste Bernard Kouemo Yanghu (awarded posthumously) Best Artistic Achievement in Documentary: Bardi by Tala Hadid Best Artistic Achievement in Narrative: Filipiñana by Rafael Manuel Best Documentary : Concrete Land by Asmahan Bkerat Best Narrative : A Girl Unknown by Zou Jing FIPRESCI Prize : Concrete Land by Asmahan Bkerat International Short Film Competition: Special Mention: Nothing Happens After Your Absence byIbrahim Omar Best Performance: Damián López for his performance in For the Opponents Best Director: Maryam Tafakory for Ghazal-e Sorkh Best Film: Whispers of a Burning Scent by Mo Harawe Made in Qatar Competition: Special Mention: Ghafleh by Tony El Ghazal Abdulaziz Jassim Award for Best Performance : Amneh Aldam – Light to Ashes by Nadia Al-Khater Best Director : Sebastian Delascasas – In the Silence After Best Film : Crawling Into Myself by Hamad Al-Fayhani Ajyal Film Competition: Best Short Film: We Were Here by Pranav Bhasin Best Feature Film: We Are Aliens by Kohei Kadowaki Audience Award: Jodari Meno by Dr Jamal Rashid Alkhanji ‘Sunrise On The Reaping’ Firing Up Thanksgiving With $85M+ Five-Day Haul Melissa Gilbert Thanks Those Who Supported Husband Timothy Busfield Broadway Will Perform Saturday In Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade New Book Alleges Former Disney Chief Iger Impregnated Employee Read More About: Comments

title: ‘Club Kid’ Star Reggie Absolom on His Friendship With Jordan Firstman and Missing Out on a ‘Harry Potter’ Role: ‘J.K. Rowling Is a No Anyway’
full_text: Nov 27, 2026 10:05am PT ‘Club Kid’ Star Reggie Absolom on His Friendship With Jordan Firstman and Missing Out on a ‘Harry Potter’ Role: ‘J.K. Rowling Is a No Anyway’ By Isabelle Farina Plus Icon Isabelle Farina Latest ‘GTA 6′ Developer Rockstar Games’ Workers Vote Against Union Recognition (Gaming News Roundup) 2 hours ago What’s New on Netflix for December 2026 22 hours ago Mike Plante, Sundance Film Festival Shorts Programmer, Dies at 56 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy Everett Collection Walking the red carpet at the Cannes Film Festival and receiving a seven-minute standing ovation is an emotional event for anyone — but especially when you’re 14, and it’s your first time acting in a feature film. Such was the case for “ Club Kid ” star Reggie Absolom . But Absolom was determined to appear as cool, calm and collected as the blue waters of the Mediterranean Sea. “ Jordan Firstman was on my left, Cara Delevingne was on my right, and I was crying so much,” Absolom tells Variety about standing through the applause that followed the film’s premiere screening. “The first thing Cara says to me, she looks at me and goes, ‘I know you were crying,’ because I was trying to hold the tears because I knew cameras were on me.” Related Stories Robert Pattinson’s Bond Ascent: How Pricey Screen Tests and Amazon Execs Landed a Starry 007 How to Get Started on Making a Difference as Tax Rules for Charitable Giving Change Despite the crowd’s cheers, it wasn’t until Absolom found out that A24 (his preference, “because they do pretty good things for indie movies”) had outmaneuvered the competition (with a whopping bid of $17 million) that he fully realized, “OK, people like this film.” That’s a little bit of an understatement. “Club Kid” was nominated for best feature at the Gothams and has delivered impressive box office numbers since its limited release on Nov. 6; in its second week in theaters, Firstman’s film tallied an impressive $28,002 per-screen average. To date, “Club Kids” has grossed more than $5 million globally. In the film, Absolom plays Arlo, the 10-year-old son of a washed-up party promoter named Peter (Firstman), whose excessive drug habits end his tenure running New York City’s queer nightlife scene. When Arlo shows up on his father’s doorstep, they are both forced to grow up and figure out how to navigate the rest of their lives. The teenage British actor won the role after auditioning for HBO’s upcoming “ Harry Potter ” series. Absolom reached the final stage of auditions to join the wizarding world, but didn’t get the job. So, U.K. casting director Lucy Bevan mentioned him to her fellow casting director Carmen Cuba, who had been searching for the perfect youngster to play Arlo. Aside from the fact that both boys are British, Absolom and his character seem to have quite a bit in common. “I love to get good at things,” Absolom says, listing the similarities between himself and Arlo, whose artistic aspirations are focused on DJing, instead of acting. “Obviously, getting there is a bit annoying, because I want to be good at everything the first time I try it. But even if I’m not, I will keep doing it until I am good at it.” Read on to find out how a potential 10 years in Hogwarts turned into 26 days immersed in New York City’s indie sleaze scene, what Absolom learned from filming his first major movie and how he’s processing the Oscar buzz. So far, you’ve been getting tons of great reviews. What’s something that someone said to you that has really meant a lot? I don’t remember the exact words, but someone told me that having this performance as a kid shows that I will only get better. And someone told me that this is one of the performances of the year. That meant loads. You’ve been on the festival circuit for a little bit; who is a celebrity or someone that you’ve met who you can’t believe has seen the movie? Josh Hutcherson. He was with Jordan in New York. He sat behind me in the screening, and he seemed like he was really enjoying it. You also get to go to all these fun after-parties. How do they compare to the parties that we see in the movie? I mean, they’re pretty fun. I don’t stay for ages because I like to get myself a good night’s sleep, but I walk around, talk to people a bit, maybe have some Diet Coke or something like that. But they’re pretty fun. The music’s actually always pretty good. Are you DJing at any of these after parties? I DJed in London, which was really fun. It’s a really cool club because you have to walk through this fully graffitied-up tunnel to get to it. Did you have to learn how to DJ for the movie? I learned during the movie, with Saturn Risin9. In the scene where she’s teaching me, she’s actually teaching me how to do things. Do you think there will be more DJing in your future? Hopefully, I think it’d be really fun. What was your first impression of all these clubs? Do you think you’ll be a clubber in the future? I mean, not like Peter or anything like that. I won’t be going weekly. Maybe once every month or two with a good group of friends could be fun. Let’s go back to the beginning. When you read the script for “Club Kid,” what did you find interesting about Arlo? The fact that he can let out so much emotion all at once. And then the next day, he wants to be such a good son, so he makes Jordan the playlist that they can add to together because he really wants to be a good kid so much, even though his parents before weren’t so good to him. Speaking of playlists, what songs were on that original playlist that Jordan sent you before the audition? “Sex with Me” by Rihanna. That was on the top. I remember that. Basically, all the songs that are in the film. There were a few more songs that when I first listened to them, I was like, “Oh, I’m not sure.” Now I’m like, “Oh my God, some of these are my favorite songs.” What was it like meeting Jordan for the first time? He seemed like a really kind guy, and the directions that he gave me during the auditions were really easy to understand and really easy to accomplish. So, I was really happy that I might be able to work with a director who can give me simple, easy-to-understand directions, instead of using big words in a direction that aren’t needed when you could just put it simpler. [It] will just make it harder for the actor to do it because they might be overthinking it. That’s what he never wanted anyone to do: overthink doing the lines. He just said, “Just do it how you would.” How has your friendship evolved since? We are super good friends after this whole press tour. This has only strengthened our bond, because we would have such random conversations and laugh about the stupidest things on set, like memes that we found on TikTok that we both know and we still do. There are so many things, so many references that we’ll say to each other that we just laugh about way too much before an interview. I bet there’s some interviews that are out there where we’re holding back laughter at the very beginning because we had just said something really stupid before the person walked in. What was your first day on set like? The first day is blocked out of my memory because all I remember is the second day, which is the throwing-up scene. Second day, and they make me throw up on camera. Not a good first impression. The pizza that we ate was nice. It was pretty good, but then they had to blend it up with applesauce. It was cold but also warm; it was lumpy as hell, and it kind of stank too. There was a cup of it next to me because I had to drink it just before. Record, “Action!” And then they were like, “Wait, wait, wait! We need to move the slide.” I was like, “I have it in my mouth, guys. Hurry up!” And then I swear, I wish someone had taken a photo of me after every take to see how the color drained from my face because I was genuinely gonna be sick if I didn’t take a break. After the third take, I was like, “Guys, give me a break. I’m sitting outside. Just give me a second.” You spend most of the movie with adults instead of people your age. How did you balance being so mature but still being a kid? I hadn’t been on set for that long — to the point where I’d been around adults for five weeks straight, not talking to kids. I had a PlayStation in my apartment so I would play with my friends. I would talk to them, and I could act like a kid because I wasn’t just around adults. Do you see any similarities between yourself and Arlo? The music taste has to be one. But Arlo also seems like he wants to be, like, a really good DJ and he really wants to be good at skateboarding. And I love to be good. I love to get good at things. Obviously, getting there is a bit annoying because I want to be good at everything the first time I try it. But even if I’m not, I will keep doing it until I am good at it. In an interview, Jordan mentioned that you’re more into hard rock music , like Metallica and Slipknot. How did you get into those bands? Because I used to play football, like what you call soccer [Absolom puts on an American accent] , and on the way, because my dad was driving me, he played “Freak on a Leash” by Korn. I was like, “OK, this is making me feel something that I’ve never felt before.” It was like anger, but good anger. It was weird. But then I was like, “OK, I need to get more of this in my playlist” and I deleted all the ’90s and 2000s rap that I had in my playlist, swapped it out for metal and then recently swapped it out for Cocteau Twins. Besides them, who’s at the forefront of your music taste? Cocteau Twins. Part Time. You heard of them? No? No one has. It says they have 300,000 monthly listeners and I haven’t met a single one of them. Pinback. Earth, Wind and Fire. The song that’s like “the 21st night of September.” Gotcha. You can make me a playlist. OK! Yeah, Jordan and I have one. [The pair’s collaborative playlist was released on Spotify .] Awesome. Now back to the movie. The ending is so emotional with their plan for a potential reunion. How do you think that reunion went? If you could write that scene, what would it look like? Well, I feel like they go out somewhere, Oscar, Peter, Arlo, as a family, kind of. I don’t know where they would go. Where’s a place that they’d all like to go? I feel like Nicky (Eldar Isgandarov) and Evelyn (Colleen Camp) are there for some reason. I feel like they want to tag along because maybe they just have a day out. Maybe they go to Times Square or something for a day. And then I feel like just Arlo and Peter go to a record store again. What do you want audiences to take away from Arlo? That no matter what’s happened to you, if you’ve had maybe a bad year, maybe you’ve had a bad few years, you’ve still got your whole life ahead of you. Don’t throw it away just because of the few bad years that you’ve had. You definitely have that wisdom that we see in Arlo. That was very wise. There is also a ton of Oscar buzz for this movie. What do you imagine that experience would be like if you got to go to the Oscars? Oh my gosh! I’d be happy if we got nominated for one award, no matter how big it is. I’d be so happy if I got nominated for any award. Obviously, winning is a humongous bonus, but I’d just be happy to be there and experience it. Winning isn’t the most important thing, but it would be fun. I like to win. What would your dream Oscars night look like? Definitely bringing my mom, of course, because she’s like my [personal assistant] as well as my mom. Definitely bring my dad too. How many plus-ones do I get? I think my sister would want to come, maybe just to be in the place. Maybe not so much for me, but she would want to come for me and to see it. Probably just my real close family and one of my aunts because she is obsessed. She’s like, “Can I chaperone you? Can I come with you?” I feel like I’d bring her because she’s obsessed with New York, and I feel like she’d love L.A. as well. So, what kind of role do you want to play next? I just want to do new stuff, like anything that comes to me, really. So, like, I’m not 100% sure what will come next. Do you think there could be a different “Harry Potter” character down the road? “Harry Potter” is out the window. “Harry Potter” got me here, and I thank it for that. But I think we don’t worry about it anymore. Looking back, are you kind of happy you didn’t get the Harry Potter role? Or did you want both? I’d rather do this. “Harry Potter” would have been a cool set to be on because it would have looked cool, but there would have been so many more people; I wouldn’t have gotten to bond with everyone. I loved everyone on this set. I had such a good time filming it, and I think J.K. Rowling’s a no anyway, but Jordan is a big yes. This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity. title: Sebastian Stan Says ‘Thunderbolts’ Had ‘More Nuance’ Than ‘Some of the Recent’ Marvel Movies and Was a ‘Success’ Despite Disappointing Box Office
full_text: × Nov 27, 2026 10:03am PT Sebastian Stan Says ‘Thunderbolts’ Had ‘More Nuance’ Than ‘Some of the Recent’ Marvel Movies and Was a ‘Success’ Despite Disappointing Box Office By Jordan Moreau Plus Icon Jordan Moreau Latest Sebastian Stan Says ‘Thunderbolts’ Had ‘More Nuance’ Than ‘Some of the Recent’ Marvel Movies and Was a ‘Success’ Despite Disappointing Box Office 33 minutes ago The Killers Guitarist Dave Keuning Survived ‘Major Stroke’ With ‘40% Chance of Survival’: ‘I Can Play Guitar Just as Good as Before’ 1 hour ago Thanksgiving Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Rules With $11.6 Million, ‘Focker-in-Law’ Follows With $7.7 Million 2 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Marvel Studios Marvel veteran Sebastian Stan is sticking up for last year’s “ Thunderbolts ,” despite it being one of the lowest-grossing MCU movies. In the team-up movie, he reprised his role as Bucky Barnes, aka the Winter Soldier, alongside Florence Pugh as Yelena Belova and David Harbour as the Red Guardian to form the Thunderbolts, a new group in the MCU. They later renamed themselves the New Avengers, made up of Wyatt Russell as U.S. Agent, Lewis Pullman as Sentry and Hannah John-Kamen as Ghost, and the team will return in next month’s “Avengers: Doomsday.” Related Stories How to Get Started on Making a Difference as Tax Rules for Charitable Giving Change Robert Pattinson’s 007 Announcement on Social Media Proves Amazon Is Already Changing the Bond Franchise After releasing in May 2025, “Thunderbolts” ended its box office run with $382 million worldwide, ranking as the fifth lowest total out of all 38 MCU films. The only movies below it are “Black Widow” ($379 million), “Captain America: The First Avenger” ($370 million), “The Incredible Hulk” ($264 million) and “The Marvels” ($206 million). They’re all a far cry from this summer’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which is the second biggest MCU movie with $2.5 billion (behind the highest-grossing film ever, “Avengers: Endgame” with $2.94 billion). “I think it’s just when you’ve had a studio and you’ve had Marvel and it’s been so many years where they’ve just been knocking it out of the park, $350 million global, something like that, it just suddenly doesn’t seem that much,” Stan said on “Next Big Picture.” “But it’s insane how much money that is.” He added, “For us, it felt like a success. I know a lot of care went into that and it had more nuance to it in terms of some of the recent ones, from my point of view at least, dealing with real issues like mental health and depression and so on.” “Thunderbolts” was praised by fans and critics for its darker tone and how it elevated its cast of misfit, lesser-known characters. Its director, Jake Schreier, was tapped by Marvel to helm its 2028 “X-Men” movie, with a cast including Sadie Sink, Adam Driver, Inde Navarrette, Kit Connor and more. title: Monica Bellucci on Challenging Hollywood Ageism in James Bond, Working With Mel Gibson and the Power of Onscreen Nudity: ‘It’s Like a Costume That Brings a Role to Life’
full_text: × Nov 27, 2026 10:01am PT Monica Bellucci on Challenging Hollywood Ageism in James Bond, Working With Mel Gibson and the Power of Onscreen Nudity: ‘It’s Like a Costume That Brings a Role to Life’ By Elsa Keslassy , Anna Tingley Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images Monica Bellucci , the glamorous Italian star who broke through internationally with “Malena” and “Irreversible,” was 50 when she made James Bond history as the oldest woman to play a Bond girl in Sam Mendes’ “Spectre.” But rather than marking the twilight of her career as a Hollywood sex symbol, the movie ushered in a new chapter for Bellucci whose career has been enjoying a second wind in recent years. Related Stories Robert Pattinson’s Bond Ascent: How Pricey Screen Tests and Amazon Execs Landed a Starry 007 Robert Pattinson’s 007 Announcement on Social Media Proves Amazon Is Already Changing the Bond Franchise During a candid, wide-ranging masterclass moderated by Variety at the Marrakech Film Festival , Bellucci recalled that Mendes really “wanted to show a mature woman, and I thought it was a beautiful idea.” “He told me, ‘Listen, I have a strong and unusual role that’s going to be surprising, a little revolutionary,” she said. “I was 50, and I had never seen a 50-year-old Bond woman. So I think I’m the oldest James Bond woman, lady or girl that we’ve ever seen,” Bellucci said with a laugh in front of a huge crowd of locals and film students who queued for over two hours to get in. Ultimately, “Spectre” and Emir Kusturica’s “On the Milky Road,” in which she starred opposite the Serbian filmmaker, came at a pivotal moment in her life. “Suddenly, I had two very strong roles. Those two films helped me get through the transition of turning 50, which wasn’t easy for an actress,” she said. Bellucci, whose body of work has largely been shaped by celebrated male auteurs — from Francis Ford Coppola to Giuseppe Tornatore, Gaspar Noé and David Lynch — also noted that she has enjoyed working with more female directors in recent years. She cited Alice Rohrwacher with her Cannes-prizewinning “The Wonders,” Rebecca Miller with “The Private Lives of Pippa Lee,” Kaouther Ben Hania with “The Man Who Sold His Skin” and Léa Mysius’ “Birthday Girl,” which competed at this year’s Cannes. “When I was younger, there weren’t as many female directors as there are today. It’s new to have so many female directors, screenwriters and even technicians on a set, so many women. We’re witnessing something completely new,” she said. “It’s another way of telling stories, sometimes another vision. And between women, sometimes there’s this ‘je ne sais quoi,’ as we say in France. Suddenly, we look at each other and, without words, we express ourselves and we understand each other. So I also really like working with women whenever possible.” Bellucci said the roles she is being offered have also evolved as she’s gotten older, allowing her to explore facets of herself that she couldn’t have accessed earlier in her career. “Our body is our working instrument. So the instrument changes and, consequently, the roles change. It’s another part of ourselves that’s expressing itself,” she said. “As we get older, we also gain experience, and we have another way of telling the story of life.” Bellucci, who made her debut on stage in 2019 with the solo show “Maria Callas: Letters and Memoirs” — which she toured in different countries and played in French, Italian and English — said she felt lucky that “times have changed and there’s a lot of respect for women in cinema.” “In the ’40s, ’50s and ’60s, it was very difficult for a woman over 40 to have a career, even if she was very talented and still had everything it took. And today that has changed.” She cited Susan Sarandon, Judi Dench, Jamie Lee Curtis and Meryl Streep as actors who have paved the way for women to continue playing compelling roles as they age. “There are magnificent actresses who are absolutely fearless,” she said, singling out Streep. “She’s so fearless and she’s incredible. There are several actresses who are free in that sense.” Bellucci also reminisced about her defining role in Giuseppe Tornatore’s 2000 drama “Malena,” which earned two Oscar nominations. Bellucci plays a young woman whose beauty triggers desire and eventually violence in a small Sicilian town during World War II. Bellucci, who says she was already a film buff from a young age “watching three films a day,” had met the Oscar-winning director of “Cinema Paradiso” during her modeling years in Italy and worked with him on a commercial for Dolce & Gabbana. Four years later, while Bellucci was shooting “Under Suspicion” with Gene Hackman and Morgan Freeman, Tornatore called to offer her the lead role which he wrote for her. “The script was already very powerful because it tells the story of women living in a man’s world, the difficulty of those relationships, the violence. It’s about a woman who finds herself alone in a man’s world and has to deal with it. Ultimately, it’s still a very contemporary film,” she said. At the time, Bellucci had already broken through in France with “L’Appartment,” starring opposite Vincent Cassel, and “Malena” represented a daring role which required a great deal of nudity and some intimate scenes with a teenage actor. She said approached these scenes “very naturally.” “I came from fashion, so I had a freedom with my body that came from the work I had done before,” Bellucci said. “Even today, I think nudity can serve to bring a character to life. When I see films like ‘Anora’ or ‘Poor Things,’ these are films where the actresses’ bodies are very important in bringing the characters to life.” “When you play a role, if nudity is part of that role, it’s simply a working tool. It’s not a way of exposing yourself. In fact, it’s like a costume that brings a role to life.” During the conversation, Bellucci also talked about her experience shooting Mel Gibson’s highly controversial blockbuster “The Passion of the Christ,” in which she portrayed Mary Magdalene. “I had another action film at the same time, and I chose ‘The Passion of the Christ’ because I wanted to work with Mel Gibson. I’d seen films of his that I liked, and it was an experience I wanted to have.” She said she had no regrets about making the 2004 biblical epic, which sparked controversy over its graphic violence and portrayal of Jewish figures, and went on to gross over $611 million worldwide. “I think every time a film sparks a discussion, it means it was important to make it. Because discussing and exchanging ideas — that’s the power of cinema,” she said. She said she approached the role Mary Magdalene as “a simple, human woman who experiences something greater than herself, something she can’t really explain. There is a form of spirituality in everyone.” Although the film didn’t bring her closer to her Catholic upbringing, she said she felt “there is never anything bad in religions. It’s the political use of religion that is dangerous.” Bellucci also praised Gibson for being “really incredible with actors on set” and revealed she had talked to him about the two-part follow up, “The Resurrection of the Christ,” which he’s currently filming. “Yes, we spoke,” she said of the sequel, adding: “I think he’s a great director.” During the masterclass, Bellucci also revisited the memorable scene in “The Matrix Reloaded” in which her character, Persephone, demands that Neo — played by Keanu Reeves — kiss her as if he were kissing Trinity (Carrie-Anne Moss) in exchange for her help. Asked whether she had to do numerous takes of the kissing scene with Keanu Reeves, Bellucci quipped, “It’s not tiring, is it? You can do it.” “He’s someone who is very gentle, respectful. We met on ‘Dracula’ and saw each other again years later on ‘The Matrix,’“ she said of Reeves. Despite landing supporting roles in several Hollywood movies at the height of her international breakthrough, Bellucci said she never felt the desire to relocate to the U.S. “I like America. I love all these possibilities, all this energy, the possibility of making big films as well as independent films. And I like going there. But I feel profoundly European. I live between Paris and Rome, and I love that,” she said. “The more time passes, the more I realize that I adore my profession and I still have that passion. But I also love the real things in my life. I love having my friends, I love my family. I also love having a kind of everyday life, something that keeps me connected to something real,” she said. “I like cinema, but I prefer life.” Among her more recent Hollywood outings was Tim Burton’s “Beetlejuice Beetlejuice,” in which she plays Delores, Beetlejuice’s vengeful, soul-sucking ex-wife who comes back from the dead to hunt him down. Bellucci said Burton’s drawings of Delores helped her envision the character. “He expresses so many things through his drawings and he had made a magnificent drawing of this character. I was already really inspired by that,” she said. “With all her scars, Delores is a bit of a parody of existence, a metaphor for life,” she said, adding that the role necessitated three hours of makeup every day. “We all have scars. We have to face them, continue to live with them and move forward.” Speaking of the scene in which she reassembles her body, she said “there were special effects, but it was also a bit like a a macabre dance.” Bellucci, who also worked with Ben Hania and Moroccan-Belgian directing duo Adil El Arbi and Bilall Fallah on “Seven Dogs,” was also upbeat about the new generation of Arab filmmakers. “There’s a lot happening. This festival is proof of that, isn’t it? All these first and second films, these incredible young filmmakers, beautiful films like ‘Adam’ and ‘The Blue Caftan.’ Beautiful things are reaching international audiences, the Cannes Film Festival and beyond. Long live cinema!“ She concluded the masterclass with a rallying cry for the moviegoing experience. “I hope cinema will never disappear because I truly believe in cinema as one of the cultural elements that are essential to humanity,” she said. ‘NCIS: New York’ Sells Across 135 Markets Globally (EXCLUSIVE) LL Cool J Announces ‘Rock the Bells: The Residency’ for Las Vegas in Spring 2027 Loading comments...

title: ‘Summer Meadow’ Directors Confront ‘Hypocrisy’ in Films About Migrants: ‘It’s as Though Black and Arab People Are Forbidden to Dream’
full_text: × Nov 27, 2026 9:50am PT ‘Summer Meadow’ Directors Confront ‘Hypocrisy’ in Films About Migrants: ‘It’s as Though Black and Arab People Are Forbidden to Dream’ By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest Doha Film Festival Showcases Five Projects From Qatar’s Industry as Local Filmmakers Hail Start of a ‘Golden Era’ 2 hours ago Mario Van Peebles, Abderrahmane Sissako Set for Ivory Coast’s SICA as African Content Economy Takes Center Stage 1 day ago Ivory Coast’s SICA Market Looks to Turn Africa’s Creative Talent Into Economic Opportunity 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Michigan Films The seemingly unremarkable movement of flocks of sheep across the French Alps took on a deeper significance for filmmakers Naël Khleifi and Lisa Debauche . The animals could freely cross borders that certain human beings could not. That observation was among the starting points for “Summer Meadow,” which explores migration, the complexities of exile and the universal desire to discover the world against a backdrop of the quiet rhythms of pastoral life. Related Stories Robert Pattinson’s 007 Announcement on Social Media Proves Amazon Is Already Changing the Bond Franchise How to Get Started on Making a Difference as Tax Rules for Charitable Giving Change “There are shepherds in Lebanon, in Palestine, in France. They’re everywhere,” Debauche says. “There’s something in that timelessness that allowed us to question contemporary issues without confining the film to current events.” Following an award-winning run at Locarno and the Cairo Film Festival, the Belgian-French feature screened at the Doha Film Festival in the Ajyal Feature Film Competition, judged by a youth jury. The film follows Hana ( Manal Issa ), a young Lebanese apprentice shepherdess who seeks refuge in the French Alps. Her encounters with fellow shepherdess Lisa (Sibylle Bataille) and a Moroccan migrant, Kebir (Elkebir Belfatmi), gradually draw her out of her isolation. For Khleifi, a Belgian-Palestinian filmmaker whose 2021 documentary “Alpes” followed residents and activists secretly helping migrants cross the French-Italian border by night, pastoral life offered another means of exploring migration, freedom and the exploitation of humans and nature. In challenging conventional narratives of migration, Khleifi identified with Kebir’s journey, driven as much by curiosity and a desire to discover the world as by a search for economic opportunities. “It’s something I know from within,” he tells Variety . “My father’s desire to leave Palestine came from a place that pushed him to leave for many reasons, but also from a desire to discover the world.” Khleifi contrasts the portrayal of European immigrants in Western cinema with that of Black and Arab migrants. “It’s as though Black and Arab people are forbidden to dream. It drives me crazy,” he says, exasperated. “At some point, we have to turn the question back on the West and confront its hypocrisy. This film is a cry. We’re human beings too. Everyone has the right to dream.” “Each story is different and rich, each journey, each feeling experienced, each past,” adds first-time director Debauche. “We so often put people into categories. We shut them in boxes, and with this film we wanted to break those boxes open.” The filmmakers also sought to blur the boundaries between documentary and fiction. “In ‘Alpes,’ I tried to break away from the conventions of documentary filmmaking, particularly the way migration is so often depicted,” Khleifi explains. “Here, I thought to myself, ‘We’re going to make a fiction film using the techniques of documentary.’ It’s a continuation of my cinematic exploration.” Though meticulously written, the screenplay continued to evolve throughout production. During 10 days of preparation before filming, conversations with Issa helped deepen Hana’s character, while Debauche encouraged first-time actress Bataille to move beyond scripted dialogue and speak in her own words. Those exchanges, Debauche notes, gave the film an added measure of soul. “We can spend months, years writing, trying to get as close as possible to a character. But reality is always much stronger than fiction.” She goes on, “Our conversations brought us so much, shifted something in us, too, and contributed to the depth of the characters and the story.” The filmmakers also resisted the temptation to explain their characters’ every motivation. “There’s something beautiful about leaving certain things unexplained,” observes Debauche. “It allows viewers to bring their own questions to the film and find their own meaning in the story.” Hana’s search for refuge, in Khleifi’s view, reflects a broader sense of unease that characterizes modern life. “With the climate crisis, wars, the far right, capitalism and this collective anxiety, we’re all a little messed up,” he says. “Everyone is trying to find a place where they can come up for air.” Before joining the project, Issa had grown disillusioned with the film industry’s response to the war in Gaza and began questioning whether she wanted to continue making films. “In films, we’re always talking about human beings. All of a sudden, children are dying in atrocious ways and we don’t want to talk about it anymore,” Issa laments. “I found myself asking why I was doing this. Had I spent years of my life doing a job where you’re afraid to say, ‘Stop killing children’?” “Summer Meadow” gave Issa both the freedom to express herself and an opportunity to rethink her craft. Working alongside nonprofessional actors and the flocks of sheep allowed her to relinquish control, an experience she likens to an acting workshop, adding that she would carry those lessons into future projects. “With the sheep, you can’t say, ‘Now I’m going to position myself like this,’” she explains. “I wanted to be out of control. For me, acting is being.” Having left Lebanon for France at 13, Issa found herself reconsidering her own relationship with freedom through conversations with Belfatmi about his experience of migration. “For me, I had been torn away from my country. All I wanted was to come back,” she recalls. “But had I really experienced life?” As Khleifi and Debauche edited the film in Europe, Issa was in Beirut amid the Israeli bombardment of the Lebanese capital, a reality that informed their decision to close the film with images of Lebanon. The friendship between Hana and Lisa, Debauche believes, speaks to the importance of being genuinely available to others. “I think it’s through our encounters with others that we perhaps come closer to ourselves,” she reflects. “These two women have very different stories. At first glance, apart from the sheep and their work, what could they possibly share? And yet, a sense of trust develops between them that allows them to make peace with certain things.” Issa experienced that firsthand. Increasingly isolated since the onset of the war, she found solace in her friendship with the filmmakers. Debauche encouraged her to share her experiences, both in conversation and on paper, some of which found their way into the screenplay. “I lived through the same thing Hana did. That’s what’s beautiful. The film came at the right time in my life. It was as though Lisa Debauche was for me what Lisa in the film was for Hana. It opened me up, made me speak out more.” ‘NCIS: New York’ Sells Across 135 Markets Globally (EXCLUSIVE) LL Cool J Announces ‘Rock the Bells: The Residency’ for Las Vegas in Spring 2027 Loading comments...

title: Denis Villeneuve Pledges Traditional, “Unapologetic” Bond: “Not Here to Change the DNA”
full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All November 27, 2026 9:47am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Robert Pattinson as James Bond for Amazon MGM Studios. Jaap Buitendijk Logo text Denis Villeneuve says his highly anticipated reboot of the James Bond franchise isn’t going to back away from the “unapologetic” traits of the iconic character. The Dune: Part Three director teased his vision of 007 in a new interview and suggested that he’s a traditionalist when it comes to portraying Ian Fleming’s suave, seductive, killer spy. “I love traditions,” Villeneuve told Time . “I love the unapologetic way the character behaves, the panache. I’m not here to change the DNA of James Bond. I’m here to embrace it, to bring it to the world of today. I’m a hardcore James Bond fan, and I want other fans to have fun watching my film. Of course, it will be tainted by my sensibility. But I wake up every morning with a stupid smile because it’s a world of pure cinematic pleasure.” Related Stories Movies 'Twilight' Director Reveals Robert Pattinson Inspired James Bond Line in 2008 Film: "We Were Seeing the Future" Movies 'Avengers: Doomsday' Eyes $270M Opening as 'Dune: Part Three' Also Heads for Big Start That said, the director added, “I don’t want to talk too much about Bond because it’s still in the oven cooking. This stage of the process is my favorite part because everything is possible.” The comments are interesting because of the cultural debate that’s surrounded Bond in recent years, and how the later Daniel Craig films attempted to wrestle with the question of how the often sexist cinematic character dating back to the 1960s should operate in the modern age. How much Villeneuve was thinking of Pattinson during his comments is unclear — the interview was conducted one week before The Batman actor was publicly announced as the new Bond . Meanwhile, speculation has shifted to who will play the film’s villain, with oddsmakers thinking Tom Hardy has a strong shot (indeed, given Pattinson’s slight frame, choosing a physically imposing villain would make for a nicely formidable antagonist). Director Danny Boyle — who was originally tapped to direct No Time to Die — has said that “beginning to talk about Jack O’Connell as a possible villain.” O’Connell was previously considered a contender to play Bond himself . Boyle told The Alchemy podcast that both Pattinson and O’Connell have a similar quality. “They have that thing [where] you want to watch them,” he said. “And it’s impossible to quantify what it is; otherwise we’d all buy it for ourselves. But it’s just there and you want to follow them.” THR

With the third film, he thought he and Warner Bros were out of the woods. Then came news that Disney was dropping into the same release weekend with Avengers . Dune is not a mammoth like the Avengers, but it’s a sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower, and I hope we will survive. title: Record Store Day Black Friday’s Most Wanted, 2026: Beatles, Noah Kahan, Bruce Springsteen, Prince, Sombr, Billy Joel, Katseye and Other Vinyl Must-Finds
full_text: × Nov 27, 2026 9:22am PT Record Store Day Black Friday’s Most Wanted, 2026: Beatles, Noah Kahan, Bruce Springsteen, Prince, Sombr, Billy Joel, Katseye and Other Vinyl Must-Finds By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest U2 Salutes Dolly Parton With Recreation of Their ‘Torn’ Duet in NFL Thanksgiving Eve Halftime Show 2 days ago Taylor Swift, a Brenda Lee Superfan, Presents the Star With 10x Platinum Plaque for ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree’ 4 days ago Ateez Debuts at No. 1 on Billboard 200 for the Third Time This Year; U2’s ‘Carnaval de Luz’ Bows at No. 4 5 days ago See All Record Store Day Record Store Day is back in black. As you likely already know, RSD is a semiannual holiday for vinyl hounds, with the Black Friday edition being a less jam-packed adjunct to the primary event in April — meaning that, this year, for instance, there are “only” 188 titles being released, almost exactly half of the 355 exclusives that were put on sale in the spring event. Even with that lesser amount of limited-edition discs going out onto the shelves, there is truly something for everybody in this list. Or, to put it another way: If you can’t find anything that grabs you in this lineup, then, to quote Leonard Cohen, you don’t really care for music, do ya? Our best guess is that there will not be utter pandemonium in the indie shops or in the lines outside this Black Friday morning, if only because of the lack of a Taylor, Olivia or Billie title this time. Which does not mean that there will not still be a healthy contingent of young people joining the veteran vinyl geeks in the checkout lines. In an interview published earlier in the week in Variety , RSD co-founder Michael Kurtz said that the majority of customers for Record Store Day events are under 35. That may continue to be the case as this one has titles from hot and/or younger-skewing artists or franchises including Noah Kahan, Katseye, Sombr and the “Wicked” and “Kpop Demon Hunters” films. That said, boomers are still gonna boom, and they, Gen-X-ers, millennials and others who have a taste for classic rock, soul and jazz — meaning every generation, really — will find something to salivate over in a list of vintage material that includes Bruce Springsteen, Prince, Joni Mitchell, Miles Davis, Billy Joel, Bill Withers, Art Blakey and even a collectible from the Beatles that was added to the list after it was first announced in October. If you want to see the entire list of 188 vinyl releases (a few of which are also having CD editions made available for the occasion) scroll all the way down. But first, if you will, look at our annotated list of 27 of the titles that we consider most covetable, ranging from Carly Rae Jepsen and Cher EPs to a 10,000 Maniacs boxed set to an expanded version of NRBQ’s classic Christmas album. Bruce Springsteen & the E Street Band, Live at Tower Theater Philly 1975 14,500 copies on 4x LP; 3,700 copies on 2x CD; black vinyl Springsteen buffs will not always agree on favorite individual shows from his and the band’s 50-year-plus history, but it’s hard to imagine a single fan not considering the “Born to Run” era to be peak form. or not taking a serious interest in this rendering of a long and loose New Year’s Eve concert at the close of 1975. The only question might be which physical format you want it in, since Sony is offering it for Record Store Day Black Friday in both LP and CD form. The much greater amount of vinyl pressed indicates an obvious consumer preference for vinyl nowadays, but with a concert this length, some may reconsider whether they want to flip sides seven times to get it all and opt for compact disc. Whether you pick up a vinyl slipcase or CD jewel box, there are succinct but sweet liner notes from Erik Flannigan, who points out that, yes, that is the band (except for Bruce) decked out in tuxedos in the photographs in the packaging. Good thing any formality about this wonderful show ends there. Noah Kahan, The Last of the Bugs 10,000 copies of vinyl 12-inch EP; Alpenglow-colored vinyl Kahan’s exclusive releases have been among the biggest draws at many recent Record Store Days, which is no surprise, given the ongoing presence of two of his studio albums in the top 10 and stadium tours that sell out instantaneously. Fans will already be familiar with the four songs on this EP — “Lighthouse,” “Staying Still,” A Few of Your Own” and “Orbiter” — since they first appeared as bonus tracks on a digital deluxe edition of his smash “The Great Divide” album (and “Orbiter” is a proper single). But having the four tracks partitioned off into their own separate physical release will be irresistible to diehard stickheads. The Beatles, Rubber Soul 15,000 copies; gold vinyl It’s not like you’re going to get any songs here that you didn’t already get on the recent “Rubber Soul” 60th anniversary super-deluxe edition… or, for that matter, that you haven’t had access to since 1966. But then, that’s the point: This single LP is a recreation of the exact album that U.S. Beatles fans got in ’66, down to the original stereo mix. But that’s been out of print for a long time… and has never been uin print as a gold-colored record, which is the main novelty here. The good news for Beatles collectors is that it’s been pressed in numbers that fall at the very top end of pressings for Record Store Day; the bad news is that 15,000 still won’t last long. Prince, 3121 Las Vegas Live 9,400 copies on 3x vinyl; 2,700 copies on 2x CD; vinyl color is crystal blue curaçao The Prince estate is really making the most out of the fact that it had a pro-shot film of Prince’s six-month 2006-7 residency in Las Vegas in the can. A film of “3121 Las Vegas Live” will briefly hit the big screen in early December, followed by a Blu-Ray edition for home consumption. In the meantime, if you want a physical manifestation of just the music, Record Store Day participant shops are the place to go. The performance captured here starts at a slow simmer but quickly heats up. Suffice it to say that, after hearing this purely audio version, I’ll be lined up for the movie. Joni Mitchell, Live At Carnegie Hall – 1972 5,000 copies; black vinyl Every time there is a new CD boxed set in the ongoing series of Joni Mitchell archival anthologies, a single live performance from that collection gets broken out to have its own separate LP edition for Record Store Day. No complaints at all about that. This ’72 concert is all Joni, accompanying herself on guitar, piano or dulcimer, all the way to a closing “Circle Game” that does have her suddenly surrounded by a chorus of famous and unfamous friends. Some will prefer Mitchell in her purest early-ish form here, and some may prefer the big band era that followed. But hearing the purity of that voice with an emphasis on the then-recent “Blue” and then-forthcoming “For the Roses” is a knockout experience. The only thing more you could wish for is a gatefold jacket instead of putting both discs in a single sleeve (the product description promises gatefold, but it’s not), or liner notes, but it’s still a handsome-looking as well as -sounding package. Billy Joel, Billy Joel Tonight 4,600 copies; black vinyl The last Billy Joel live album, released for Record Store Day Black Friday 2025, was “Live From Long Island,” pressed in a quantity of 1,500 copies — and fans are still pissed about that. (Resale copy prices are not completely exorbitant, but they do go for more than $100.) Fortunately, the record company got the message and is putting three times that many of this followup on sale, 4,600, although that still may not completely sate the market for live Joel. It’s a spirited set, from a hyperactive “Angry Young Man” opening forward, recorded Dec. 5, 1976 at Connecticut College for a TV special. It includes 15 never-before-released tracks from either the original live shows or a followup that was done to get better takes for the special. The blurb on the back cover promises that four more tracks will be included in a “Turnstiles” 50th anniversary boxed set coming out next year. But few Joel fans will complain about that wait given the wealth of heretofore unreleased music here. Sombr, In Another Life and Benson Boone, Walk Me Home… Sombr: 7,500 copies on silver vinyl Boone: 5,000 copies on black and white galaxy vinyl The Sombr and Benson Boone releases are very similar, in that each is a first-time vinyl issue of the EP that started their major-label careers before they broke a lot bigger with a full album that followed. Bot EPs are also mellower than some of the hit music that followed for these artists — Sombr lives up to his name more here. His EP, at four tracks, is less expansive than Boones, which runs to eight songs, and comes with a 12-by-24 insert that has a poster image on one side and lyrics on the other. Apart from their musical merits, both discs just look fab, pulled out of their sleeves and placed into the wild. Bill Withers, Bill Withers In Concert – Live at the BBC, 1974 , and Various Artists, Who Is He And What Is He To You? Withers: 2,600 copies on LP; 1,300 copies on CD; LP is black vinyl Various artists/Sweet Relief: 1,200 copies Now here’s an unofficial two-fer anyone should think about picking up and turning into a double feature, even if their simultaneous release, coming from different labels, may be coincidental. First, there’s Withers’ own 1974 performance, captured for British TV. You can tell the audio is unedited: Withers is heard telling the studio audience that some of his band members are out sick, and in one case restarting a speech. The relaxed feel carries over to the superlative songs. Meanwhile, I have to give an even more enthusiastic endorsement to a double-LP tribute album put together as a benefit for the Sweet Relief Foundation that includes all-new tracks. I was hoping the great Chris Pierce — one of the closest things we have to a modern-day Withers right now — would be one of the artists chosen, and to my sweet relief, he was, contributing “Better Off Dead.” There are also choice cuts from Rickie Lee Jones, Lady Blackbird, Marilyn McCoo and Billy Davis Jr., Ben Harper and others who know how to mix their own spin on things with takes that feel faithful to Withers’ vibe. Ten Thousand Maniacs, Candy Everybody Wants 2,600.copies of six-LP boxed set; multiple vinyl colors Rhino has gotten in the habit of issuing one complete boxed set per RSD event for a renowned artist from the Warner-Elektra catalog of riches, from John Prine to Devo. This one for 10,000 Maniacs, composed of all the albums the group put out before Natalie Merchant split to go solo in 1993, is being seen by fans as a very necessary corrective to the fact that a lot of that stuff has been out of print on vinyl forever. Four studio albums are joined by the pre-fame compendium “Hope Chest” and a newly assembled rarities disc full of delectable covers. Merchant is credited with helping oversee the package, including the design of the physical elements, although the liner notes (which are very good) do not include interviews with her or any of the bandmates who continue to carry on without her. It’s worth noting that all of the albums included except the rarities LP are due to be issued individually early next year, if it’s just one or two you need to pick up. But as a fan from their earliest major-label days, I couldn’t imagine not getting the whole thing right now. A matter of curiosity: All of the box and LP packaging here changes the band’s name to Ten Thousand Maniacs from 10,000 Maniacs (although the numerical usage pops up in the liner notes). Some elements of the album cover art have been changed, along with the band-name logos — it has to be a Merchant thing. But if you pick up the individual issues in a few months, apparently the name and artwork will be as we remember them. (The fact that the albums in this box have different covers is further cemented by the lack of barcodes.) Those peculiarities aside, t’s a great trip down maniacal memory lane. Carly Rae Jepsen, Day and Night (Continued) 4,000 copies Jepsen has been nothing but prolific in this era, first issuing “Day and Night” as a hefty double-album, then adding eight additional tracks onto the original 24 for a deluxe edition, “Day and Night (Continued).” that runs to an hour and 55 minutes of material. Some things may be more easily digested in smaller chunks, of course, and this EP — also titled “Day and Night (Continued)” — breaks out those eight fresher tracks and gives them their first appearance in a physical format. Plus, you get still more from her photo shoot at Eagle Rock’s Casa Bianca, the best pizza joint in L.A., and if that’s not reason enough to pick it up, you’ve got eight more. Various Artists, Wicked: The Complete Soundtrack 3.000 copies of 4x LP set The previous RSD exclusive editions of the “Wicked” and “Wicked: For Good” sold out so quickly, I never did actually catch a glimpse of either of them in my many store visits. That will probably prove true for this combined set that packages both soundtracks together in a 4-LP set in a slipcase with a poster. (The track list, if accurate as rendered online, leaves out the bonus track that was added onto the original RSD “Wicked” issue.) Good luck hunting this down, unless it turns out every franchise fan was sated by the previous two releases after all, which isn’t likely. It’s gonna be popular. Art Blakey & the Jazz Messengers, Blue Moon Over Paris – ORTF Recordings 1963-1968 3,300 2x LP copies; black vinyl The first of several releases we’ll mention here produced by “jazz detective” Zefv Feldman is a welcome incursion into the wonderful world of Blakey. It comtbines two previously unreleased performances in Paris, the first from 1963 and sporting famous players like Freddie Hubbard and Wayne Shorter, the second with a different ensemble in ’68. “Moons” were on the band leader’s mind, as the collection includes the two big musical moon shots of the era, “Blue Moon” and “Moon River.” The latter opens the collection and might give Henry Mancini a heart attack if he were still around to have one — it’s like “Moon River” on amphetamines (not speaking literally, friends, just figuratively), and it’s quite a fantastic flood. The liner notes booklet is copious as with almost any Feldman-related release, and even though a CD edition will follow for the general market in a week, it’s always worth picking up the limited-edition vinyl versions of these releases just for the larger type and photographs. And, sure, the wide-open grooves, too. The B-52s, Meso-Americans Live 1982 5,000 copies of 2x LP; on “Third Pyramid Pink” vinyl I would have taken an interest in a B-52s live set anyway, but this one turns out to be particularly a wowser because of the addition of a three-man horn section that really helps some of the songs rock in an augmented way. Fans may already know this Roseland Ballroom NYC ’82 performance from when it was included in the “Ancient Culture: Mesopotamia Revisited” set, but for those of us who didn’t have that, or anyone who did but just likes a good breakout, it’s a delightful revelation of the band at its early ’80s peak. Cher, Christmas – DJ Party Edition 3,500 copies of 12-inch vinyl EP; red vinyl Cher had not released any original material in many years until she came back with a Christmas project that included some songs newly written to add to the holiday tuneage canon. With this EP spinoff, the emphasis is on the dance-ier chestnuts, including three different mixes of “DJ Play a Christmas Song” and an added duet with Kelly Clarkson. The lady-in-red cover shot is different from any previous artwork in her Christmas-music campaign, too. Katseye, KATSEYE: The Dance Breaks 5,000 copies of single-sided EP We were not able to preview this particular release, so we cannot vouch for what the “dance break” versions of three of Katseye’s most popular songs sound like — “Debut,” “Gnarly” and “Gabriela.” But we can tell you the way it will fly off the shelves will be gnarly indeed. All three mixes are congregated on one side of the vinyl, with a mystery etching on the other. Each copy is said to includes two out of six “randomly selected unique photocards,” so fans will be figuring out how to get around the one-copy-per-customer rule in most stores, as if this needed an incentive to sell out faster. Bobby Womack, The Preacher In Paris – Live at The Elysee Montmartre 2,600 copies of 2x LP; black vinyl Another archival production from Zev Feldman, who is stretching out from being seen as “just” a jazz guy with his Bobby Womack and Marianne Faithful releases this Record Store Day. Womack can also stretch out, as it turns out, with two numbers in this live set that go past the 12-minute mark, “You’re Welcome, Stop on By” and “Communication” are both over 12 minutes long. Recorded in Paris in 1976, where the liner notes say he was having a higher profile at the time than in the U.S., this collection feels essential as a revelation of just what an expansive showman he was as well as crafter of classic soul singles. Various Artists, Kpop Demon Hunters (Soundtrack from the Netflix Film) 10,000 copies; “Derpy Sussie Splatter” vinyl The hunt for “Kpop Demon Hunters” collectibles never stops. Record Store Day just had dual editions of the soundtrack that were quick and easy sellouts, but that could hardly stand in the way of yet another version — and surely not the last — this one featuring fresh art created by official “Demon Hunters” production designer Mingjue Helen Chen and visual development artist Marion Bordeyne. We’ll let the product description do the rest of the talking: “This Derpy Sussie Splatter vinyl includes exclusive holographic art on both the front cover and triple gatefold, 3 of 6 mini inserts, 1 of 3 holographic mini inserts, a sticker sheet, and an oversized poster.” You might have to take their word for it since it won’t be surprising if most or all of the copies are gone by the time you get your lazy post-Thanksgiving butt to the shop. Stan Getz, The Sound in San Francisco: Live at Keystone Korner 3x LP; black vinyl Sax man Getz is the only one with his name above the title on this release, but for the first three of its six sides, legendary guitarist João Gilberto is his equal costar. Together, they recreate the magic they’d made together in a historic studio teaming in one of the few live shows they did together to follow that. All the music here was previously released by Resonance more than a decade ago, but this three-LP set for the first time combines two albums — one of Getz with Gilberto in SF, one without — into an exemplary single package (and the Getz-only half of the equation never made it onto vinyl before). The multiple interviews or essays in the copious liner notes even include a sizable explanation of the bossa nova craze that finds a kind of quiet culmination here. Fountains of Wayne, Sky Full of Holes – 15th Anniversary Edition 2,000 copies; “sky blue” vinyl Fountains of Wayne’s final album before their breakup sometimes gets undervalued because it’s their least comical, most sober outing, perhaps reflecting the more dominant influence of Chris Collingwood, versus the wryer touch favored by Adam Schlesinger, who’d run the show more on the preceding record. Regardless, there’s wit enough here, along with some of the band’s starker songs. It’s been challenging for FoW fans to complete their vinyl collections, since this fast went out of print after a single pressing in 2001. Even now, 2,000 is not a lot, but it’ll be at least enough to satisfy some of us who never stopped believing that this brilliant group had it going on. Miles Davis, Copenhagen Live 1969 4,400 copies; black vinyl This is the “Bitches Brew”-era Miles who took free jazz into the land of psychedelia, if you hadn’t already guessed that from the cover art by his favorite cover painter in the ’60s, Mati Klarwein. It might as well have been recorded at the Fillmore, even though Davis actually had his all-star quintet (Wayne Shorter, Chick Corea, Dave Holland and Jack DeJohnette) in Copenhagen for a TV taping. The music has previously been heard on a DVD and on a one-time vinyl pressing of just a few hundred copies, but this mastering is said to be a revelation even for the relatively small number of cultists who’ve already heard this dynamic performance in some form. Goo Goo Dolls, Borrowed 3,500 copies; on “Pawn Shop Patina”-colored vinyl As the title and cover hint, this is a collection of cover songs these Dolls have done over the years, and what great taste they’ve had in other bands, as evidenced in a collection that runs from the Plimsouls’ “A Million Miles Away” to the Kinks’ “Catch Me Now, I’m Falling,” with stops for Tom Petty, INXS, Prince and… Supertramp! (A CD and digital release will follow a week after this vinyl exclusive.) King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard, Expand Your Mind: Songs in 3D (Deluxe Edition) 5,000 copies; 3D zoetrope picture-disc vinyl We did not get a review copy of this, but we’re going to guess from the product description alone that it might be fun, with or without actually listening to what’s in the grooves, just from looking at them. “Zoetrope” discs have been a thing for a while, turning vinyl into animation, but this is the first one we can recall seeing that is billed as a 3D zoetrope disc, with cardboard glasses to put on to enjoy the effect. We look forward to hearing whether the effect of watching that is as mind-bending as the Gizzard boys’ music typically is, and what substances it is best combined with. Marianne Faithful, Eye Communication: Live at The Wax Museum 1,800 copies on three-sided 2x LP set; black vinyl We’re still morning Faithful’s passing, so it’s moving to hear her in her prime, or one of her primes, in a performance captured in 1983, after a comeback run of three acclaimed albums on Island, including of course “Broken English.” The tape of the D.C. set ends with the title track from that latter album and is missing a few final songs from the actual performance, so it’s spread across three sides and the fourth is devoted to an etching of a William Blake quote in concentric-circle script. Various Artists, Jazz Dispensary: Cosmic Nuggets 2,215 copies of six-45-rpm-singles boxed set; different marbled color variations Jazz Dispensary dispenses something worth picking up for every single RSD edition, and this time they’ve eschewed the usual single-LP compilation format to put out a box of singles. It comes in a candy-style box, with six different vintage singles in different but equally delicious-looking colors, plus some glow-in-the-dark 45 adapters as a bonus. As usual, even though the description calls these “jazz,” the music therein leans more toward the funk side of the fence, from Eddie Jefferson’s honestly groovy “Psychedelic Sally” to Patrice Rushen’s kinda-weird “Kickin’ Back.” Obscure but charming singles from Rusty Bryant, Idris Muhammad, Pleasure and Johnny Hammond are also represented. Will you play these a lot, or easily find shelf space for an odd-shaped package? Probably no in both cases, yet it’s kind of irresistible as a hep novelty package nonetheless. NRBQ, Christmas Wish (Fan Club Fun Version) 1,200 copies; opaque green vinyl What could be better for celebrating the season than NRBQ’s 1978 “Merry Christmas From NRBQ” EP? Very possibly, a modern expansion of that project that extends it to 19 tracks, 10 of them making their vinyl debut, one (the closing “Auld Lang Syne”) getting its premiere altogether. We weren’t able to preview this package to tell you whether they do or don’t rock out the newly added “Jesus Loves Me” and “The Christmas Song,” but we hope to score a copy and fill in that part of the NRB-FAQ. title: Masaaki Yuasa’s ‘Daisy’s Life’ Unveils First Look Images From Japanese Anime Giant’s Next Feature
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All November 27, 2026 9:10am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Daisy's Life' Studio ame pippin Japanese anime master Masaaki Yuasa’s new studio, ame pippin, has revealed first look images and a clip from the highly-anticipated animated feature Daisy’s Life , a tale of grief and healing now delayed to a 2027 theatrical release in Japan. The first title from Yuasa’s new studio ame pippin unveiled images to The Hollywood Reporter of the main characters from the animated adaptation of Banana Yoshimoto’s novel, The Life of Daisy, and original illustrations by Yoshitomo Nara. In one image, the young protagonist Daisy and her closest friend, Dahlia, are standing together in a lush forest. Related Stories Movies Golden Globes Category Chaos: When 'The Drama' Is a Comedy... Movies Golden Globes: 'I Play Rocky' Submitted as Comedy (Exclusive) The second image shows both animated characters seated together at the roots of a tree, bonding over yakisoba, a Japanese stir-fried noodle dish. Their friendship helps frame the story of Daisy, who, as a child, lost her mother, her only family, in a tragic accident and now grieves that death as she struggles with a new life with her aunt. Studio ame pippin on Thursday unveiled a short clip from Daisy’s Life on X. Daisy’s Life Studio ame pippin “On a long, lonely night during the rainy season, she (Daisy) plays the recorder by herself. As if drawn by the sound, Dahlia appears and becomes the friend who supports Daisy through her isolation. Years later, while Daisy is living and working at her aunt and uncle’s yakisoba restaurant, a letter arrives from Brazil. It speaks of the mysterious connection between two lonely souls separated by distance and time,” a synopsis from the producers of Daisy’s Life states about the young girl’s life changing one sleepless night. The film is the first animated feature from ame pippin, the animation studio founded by Yuasa in 2025. Daisy’s Life also marks the first animated adaptation of books by Yoshimoto, a popular Japanese writer whose literary work has been published in 30 countries, with over seven million copies in print. Published in 2000, Yashimoto’s The Life of Daisy novel centers around Daisy (Hinagiku) and explores the themes of death and loss through Daisy’s relationships with her mother and childhood best friend, Dahlia. Director Yuasa is known for classic films like The Tatami Galaxy and Ping Pong the Animation, and in 2013 co-founded Science SARU with Eunyoung Choi. He directed an episode of Adventure Time and The Night Is Short, Walk on Girl. Yuasa left Science SARU in 2020 after Keep Your Hands Off Eizouken! and directed Inu-Oh, which earned both Golden Globe and Annie nominations. Character designer Izumi Murakami created the animated characters for Yuasa’s Daisy’s Life adaptation, while production designer Tomotaka Kubo created the film’s settings that envelop Daisy and Dahlia’s time together. Visual development artist Batiste Perron, color designer Ayaka Nakamura, director of photography Yoshihiro Sekiya and editor Kiyoshi Hirose are also part of Yuasa’s creative team. The Japanese-French co-production is from ame pippin and Miyu Productions, with Fumie Takeuchi, Emmanuel-Alain Raynal and Pierre Baussaron sharing producer credits. title: Denis Villeneuve “Deeply Disappointed” Disney Put ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Against ‘Dune 3’
full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All November 27, 2026 9:04am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Zendaya in 'Dune: Part Three' Courtesy of Everett Logo text Everybody has found it pretty cute, if slightly baffling, that expected box-office heavyweights Dune: Part Three and Avengers: Doomsday are opening on the same day (Dec. 18). But Dune franchise director Denis Villeneuve isn’t amused by going head-to-head with the Marvel titan. Villeneuve explains in a new interview that he was “deeply disappointed” by the “Dunesday” scheduling, but that Warner Bros. was basically trapped in the slot because the studio had successfully secured an exclusive run on IMAX screens for Dune 3 through the December holidays. Related Stories Movies 'Avengers: Doomsday' Eyes $270M Opening as 'Dune: Part Three' Also Heads for Big Start Movies 'Avengers: Doomsday' Final Trailer Shows Major X-Men Moment “Listen, I will be honest,” he told Time . “The first Dune came out at the end of the pandemic. We made a great box office in a very rough environment. But we had the winds against us. Then the second movie, same thing. We were meant to release in the fall, and we had to release at the end of winter because of the two Hollywood strikes. We had success, but it was not easy. The third time, I said to myself, ‘Finally, there is no pandemic, no strike in sight. We will have a normal release.’ Then Disney put the biggest franchise of all time against us. I’m no fool. Those movies are a mammoth.” “So I was deeply disappointed,” continued the director. “But we had committed to this date, to IMAX. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema. Dune is not a mammoth like the Avengers, but it’s a sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower, and I hope we will survive. It could be one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time because of both movies. Am I in competition with the Avengers ? Absolutely not. It’s a T. rex. But I stand proud because I think the film delivers.” Both films have notably broken presales records . Dune: Part Three has reportedly bested Warner Bros. all-time presales record, selling more than $30 million worth of tickets for IMAX screens alone (the studio hasn’t released its own all-theater presales numbers). But Doomsday has recently surpassed $100 million and has received the highest initial opening-weekend forecast in NRG tracking history ($270 million). So there’s no world in which both films aren’t big hits, but also no world in which Doomsday doesn’t clock Dune on opening weekend. Villeneuve also defended making some significant changes to Dune saga author Frank Herbert’s source material for the third film, particularly in the storyline of Chani (Zendaya). “When you adapt, you kill,” he said. “It is not the book. It is my movie inspired by the book, with tremendous respect … I had the idea to make Chani more of a critic regarding the idea of religious colonization … In the third movie, Chani is still a critic of the choices Paul has made. She believes the Fremen should free themselves. She doesn’t want to harm Paul, but she does want to harm his regime. I would have loved to have taken Frank Herbert for a coffee about these ideas because I think he could have liked them. In the book, Chani is there to give Paul foot massages. It’s a character that has not a lot of firepower.” THR
