title: The Ultimate Thanksgiving Detox? Mexico’s Most Over-the-Top, Celeb-Approved Longevity Clinic
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ingrid Schmidt Plus Icon Ingrid Schmidt Contributor ingridschmidt_ Follow Sign Up View All November 27, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The view from one of the suites at SHA Mexico. Eduardo Martinez/SHA Mexico Pampering spa getaways are so passé. The reinvented power trip? Longevity-centered five-star resorts that zero in on preventive medicine and rigorous cutting-edge health-optimization treatments. Think Benjamin Button-like cellular reprogramming and biotech breakthroughs that promise to help rewind biological aging in the elite quest to amp up health span. Once confined largely to Switzerland, top-tier medi- wellness destinations are moving closer to Hollywood. Most notable among them is SHA Mexico, which opened in 2024 on a beachfront stretch of Costa Mujeres, north of Cancún. The flagship avant-garde longevity clinic, SHA Spain, launched in 2008 in the coastal town of L’Albir, has welcomed pro athletes, royalty, supermodels and such stars as Barbra Streisand (for repeat visits), Demi Moore, Monica Bellucci, Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz, Lily James, Madonna and Marisa Tomei. Now names like Dakota Johnson, Kate Moss, Jack Black, Pink, model Candice Swanepoel and Lake Bell are on the guest list at the Mexican outpost. Related Stories Lifestyle The 5 Best Red Light Therapy Panels for Improving Your Health At-Home Lifestyle Jennifer Aniston Joins Boyfriend Jim Curtis For Chat About Health, Wellness and Hypnotherapy Calling to mind The Jetsons ’ Googie-style home in Orbit City, the futuristic design, by Mexican architecture studio Sordo Madaleno, was aptly inspired by the human genome. Exclusive to this location is a bank of stem cells, unveiled in June, ethically sourced from embryonic tissues for medical and aesthetic cellular regeneration therapies that target autoimmune disease, muscle injuries, sleep apnea, aging skin and more. (At SHA Spain, therapies use the patient’s own stem cells; these donor-derived regenerative treatments are not yet approved in the U.S. or Europe for the uses described.) Treatments are administered through intravenous infusions, nebulizer inhalation and targeted injection; exosome facials inject the cell-derived donor particles directly into the face. “These therapies reprogram the body’s natural mechanisms to heal and rejuvenate from the inside out,” says Dr. Andrea Márquez, head of SHA’s regenerative medicine, explaining that aging or inflamed cellular systems need a reboot. The hydrotherapy pool. Eduardo Martinez/SHA Mexico The architecture of SHA Mexico, by Mexican firm Sordo Madaleno, was aptly inspired by the human genome. Eduardo Martinez/SHA Mexico A Cell Regeneration Therapy bed with a “human regenerator device” is said to boost energy, support physical recovery and promote anti-aging benefits by surrounding the body with a field of electrically charged particles. A popular European beauty secret, not yet available in the U.S. and offered at SHA Mexico, is Profhilo, the Italian hyaluronic acid-based skin remodeling injectable that improves elasticity. More than 200 SHA offerings range from neurocognitive, hormonal and sleep health to genomic medicine, dermatology and physiotherapy. Each guest is prescribed teas and an anti-inflammatory vegan or pescatarian diet, with add-ons like seaweed or shots of apple cider vinegar. SHA’s Japanese-influenced dietary rules discourage liquid drinks during meals (said to “hinder digestion”), and breakfast kicks off with a bowl of miso soup (probiotic-rich to support gut health). One gut-health package popular with the Hollywood crowd promises to detox and optimize the digestive system. Included are an intestinal dysbiosis analysis, visceral osteopathy (hands-on manipulation of the abdomen intended to improve function of internal organs) and intestinal ozone therapy. Not FDA-approved as a medical treatment in the U.S., the latter pumps an oxygen/ozone gas mixture into the rectum to purportedly “reduce oxidative stress, support immune balance and promote tissue repair,” according to the SHA website. Gwyneth Paltrow and self-proclaimed “father of biohacking” Dave Asprey have both fessed to using rectal ozone therapy. Vaginal ozone therapy and ozone IV infusions (also used by Asprey) are additionally on the service menu, as is a dental cleaning that incorporates the agent. The facility’s stem cell bank. Eduardo Martinez/SHA Mexico The wellness resort’s infinity pool. Eduardo Martinez/SHA Mexico Hollywood dermatologist Ava Shamban (whose clients include Moore, Angela Bassett, Nicole Kidman and Michelle Yeoh) weighs in on donor stem cells and ozone treatments: “I say proceed with caution. The science is soft. The good news is that we are on the cusp of truly groundbreaking longevity sciences that will come with DNA optimization and literal reversal of aging, using the newest technologies.” As over-the-top as some of this may seem, SHA’s owners are firmly at the forefront of longevity research: “It’s not just about trendy biohacking and optimization; we have built a legacy approaching longevity through the lens of both Western functional medicine and Eastern holistic practices,” says SHA managing partner Alejandro Bataller, whose father, Alfredo Bataller, was inspired to found the company after integrative medicine and nutritional shifts helped him overcome early stage colon cancer. All-inclusive rooms at SHA Mexico run $600 to $9,000 a night, plus program rates starting at $4,800 for a four-night stay. In late June, SHA’s umbrella company, AB Living Group, opened St. Regis Costa Mujeres Resort & Residences next door with a luxe spa, 24-hour butler service, daily champagne sabrage and guest access to SHA. For those who want to truly live the lifestyle, private SHA Residences start at $2.5 million. Next up is SHA Emirates (billed as “the world’s first longevity island”), slated to open in AlJurf, along the coast between Dubai and Abu Dhabi, in early 2028. Residences there will cost $27 million. title: Federal Incentive Will Level The Playing Field For America’s Creatives — Guest Column
full_text: Skip to main content By Ruth Vitale Ruth Vitale More Stories By Ruth Big Tech Shouldn’t Ignore AI’s “Turbo-Charged Threat” In Digital Piracy Battle – Guest Column View All November 27, 2026 8:27am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Al Drago/Getty Images Editor’s note: Ruth Vitale , who previously held top posts at Paramount Classics, Fine Line Features and New Line Cinema, is CEO of CreativeFuture , a nonprofit coalition of more than 500 companies and organizations and nearly 300,000 individuals devoted to promoting the value of creativity in the digital age. For more than a decade, CreativeFuture has fought for one simple idea: Members of our creative communities deserve to make a living from the work they create. We have taken on piracy. We have taken on Big Tech. We have taken on criminal enterprises that profit from the theft of our movies, television, music, and books. Related Stories News Trump's "Noisy Name-Calling" Mocked By NYT After Bored POTUS Starts Thanksgiving Ranting Against Reporter's Nvidia Dispatch News Jane Fonda, Robert De Niro & Other Figures Sign Letter Backing Chris Van Hollen For Majority Leader --- Amid A Chuck Schumer Aide's Prank But right now, America’s creative community faces a different kind of threat. Fewer movies and television shows are being produced in this country. Copyright protects creative work once it exists. It does nothing for the American crews who never got the opportunity to make it. Watch on Deadline I have spent my entire career in this business – at Vestron, where we made Dirty Dancing , and then at United Artists, Fine Line Features, and Paramount Classics, where we released films like Child’s Play , Road House, Shine, You Can Count on Me, and Hustle & Flow. I have watched independent filmmakers scrape together budgets one dollar at a time. Today, I hear the same question from filmmakers repeatedly: Can we afford to make this in America? More and more often, the answer is no. At least 65 countries now offer national production incentives, sometimes in addition to local or regional ones. The United States does not. Thirty-nine states have built programs of their own, but a state program cannot outbid a government overseas with more competitive incentives in place, and the numbers show it. America’s share of global film production has fallen from 52% in 2022, to just 38% at the start of 2026. The share was 65% just over a decade ago. Let’s be clear about who pays the price. Film and television support more than two million American jobs and pay over $200 billion in wages a year. Nationally, the industry supports 162,000 businesses, 93% of which employ fewer than 10 people. Those paychecks go to editors and composers, costume designers and carpenters, camera operators and writers’ assistants. Many of them work from project to project, with no guarantee there will be a next one. When a production moves overseas, their jobs move without them. That is why I am so encouraged by the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act (MPTERA). Introduced last month with strong bipartisan support in both chambers, it would create federal tax relief for film and television made in America based on the U.S. jobs created, including for postproduction and visual effects. Editing suites and effects houses can be anywhere in the world – which means they can just as easily be somewhere other than here. MPTERA also gives independent productions extra relief, up to 30% of the amount spent on U.S. jobs. As someone who has built much of my career championing independent film, I can tell you that matters. Independent films are where new voices are discovered, and run on margins so thin that an overseas incentive can decide whether they get shot in Albuquerque or Belfast. Or whether they get shot at all. The upside is enormous. A new study estimates that a federal incentive would support an average of more than 143,000 jobs a year and generate nearly $250 billion in additional economic activity over eight years. And this won’t help only California and New York – our industry is in every state of the union, leaving its economic mark everywhere it goes. There is also a bonus for productions in rural areas or for producers that film in at least 10 states in a year. And keep in mind, a feature film’s location shoot generates an average of $670,000 per day for local communities. For a one-hour television episode, it’s $475,000 per day. Bottom line: This is not a giveaway. Not a single taxpayer dollar goes to the production – the legislation simply reduces the tax liability of U.S. productions. It is a smart investment in one of the few industries where America still leads the world. Our film and television industry maintains a trade surplus with nearly every nation on Earth. When Americans were asked what their country does better than any other, 58% named movies and television as their top answer. Why would we let that slip away? Other countries have quickly realized the economic benefit that production brings. Standing still here at home is not a policy. It is clearly a forfeit. This is a bill that has the support of President Trump, as well as Senators Tim Scott and Adam Schiff and Reps. Nathaniel Moran and Linda Sánchez, and 90 other members of Congress. This is the rare bill that has reached across the aisle and to the White House. That doesn’t happen often. Congress should pass MPTERA this year. We already have the talent and resources and will see the benefit immediately. America’s creatives are ready to work. Let’s give them the chance to do it here at home. Ruth Vitale is the CEO of CreativeFuture, a nonprofit coalition of over 500 companies and organizations and nearly 300,000 individuals devoted to promoting the value of creativity in the digital age. title: Arthur Conti Was Booked This Year With Roles in ‘Carrie’ and ‘Ebenezer.’ Now He’s Looking to Get “a Little Strange”
full_text: × Skip to main content Arthur Conti Photography by Franco Origlia/Getty Images British actor Arthur Conti is fresh off a whirlwind year. With roles in Mike Flanagan’s Carrie adaptation and the recently released Ebenezer , he’s been busy crafting new interpretations of well-known characters. “To play an iconic character that’s been played by many people before, and to get to give your own spin on it, is very exciting,” Conti tells The Hollywood Reporter over Zoom from London about what he’s been up to this year. The 22-year-old actor is back in the U.K. after over a month of press for Carrie and Ebenezer and a stint in Portland, Oregon. “It’s been a bit of a whirlwind, but it’s been very enjoyable,” he says. After a breakout performance in 2024’s Beetlejuice Beetlejuice , 2026 has been the actor’s biggest year to date between the two projects and a role in Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma . Related Stories TV Why Mike Flanagan Just Couldn't Kill Carrie White Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Slays $120M at Box Office as Franchise Heats Back Up With Carrie , Conti stepped into the role of teen bully Billy Nolan, first played on screen by John Travolta in Brian De Palma’s 1976 film. Conti had read Stephen King’s novel but hadn’t seen De Palma’s film, which he stayed away from during filming. Conti’s Billy, while still one of the villains of the story, is different from Travolta’s take on the character. “I was worried that even inadvertently or subconsciously I would copy things about that performance, and I really wanted it to be all my own,” he says. Ebenezer finds Conti stepping into the shoes of the titular character of Ebenezer Scrooge — well, the younger version of him anyway. The actor heard that Ti West would be making the film, and as a big fan, he sent in a self-tape. Much like with Carrie , he tried not to take too much inspiration from previous versions of the story, but there’s one adaptation that stands out. “[ The Muppets version] is probably the best one. I mean, it’s amazing, that film. Michael Caine gives such a genuinely brilliant, dramatic performance in that film against the Muppets,” he says. “He takes it so seriously, and that is the beauty of that film is that you’d think he was talking to John Gielgud, and he’s talking to Fozzy.” Despite The Muppets Christmas Carol being his main experience with the story beforehand, he did watch the 1951 film adaptation starring Alastair Sim as Scrooge. “I really liked,” he notes. Below, the actor digs into his last year in roles, what he’s looking to do next and how he’d spend a perfect day in London. I’m always curious, as someone who enjoys it — have you seen Carrie: The Musical ? We watched it. We saw a theater production on Granville Island in Vancouver. It was a youth theater production of Carrie: The Musical . [The cast of Carrie ] all went to go and see it. Mike [Flanagan] actually put the cast of that production of Carrie in the show. They’re all at the prom. Throughout the show, they’re in the background at the school, which was really, really fun. Arthur Conti and Alison Thornton in Carrie . Prime Video How has the year been? You were busy with Carrie and now Ebenezer . [ Carrie ] was my first big press tour. It was my first time doing a press junket and all of these things. It feels like the biggest thing that I’ve done so far [with] how much I’ve been promoting it. It was all incredibly exciting. [In Carrie ,] I’m playing another character that has several sides to him, after [I did in] Beetlejuice. It’s another deceptively charming, manipulative character, which is interesting that I keep taking. ( Laughs ). Where do you think that’s coming from? Something about me, I don’t know. Something untrustworthy. Honestly, it is a treat to play characters like that because you get the chance to do multiple things at once, present a character that has many layers and is complex and isn’t wholly one thing or another. It was a great role. It was a really meaty role to sink my teeth into, and it was an honor to play a character of that literary significance. It was a privilege to be entrusted with that. As an actor, are you drawn to characters that are different from you, then? It’s nice to get outside of yourself — that’s part of the fun of it. Growing up, the films I was watching, I was a lot more drawn to flawed or strange or darker characters. I grew up watching Steve Buchemi in Fargo and Philip Seymour Hoffman in Punch-Drunk Love and Talented Mr. Ripley . Those are the kind of characters that I always really loved to watch. The scope of the projects you had this year has been quite large. Are you drawn to that or looking to change it? You’re right. They are quite large-scale. I think I’m drawn to things that are a little out there and a little strange. Horror is one of the best genres to explore that area because it emboldens filmmakers to experiment and take risks and be a bit weird and a bit dreamlike. That’s why I gravitate towards horror a lot, and it’s probably what I watch the most of in the cinema. Is that where you got your love for it? Were you big into horror as a kid? I think so. It’s not horror, just things that are a little strange. My mom brought me up on Charlie Kaufman films. Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind is my mom’s favorite film, so I watched that quite early. Things that tap into that dreaminess and that weirdness and spookiness — that’s up my alley. But it would be a dream to do a Before Sunrise kind of thing, where it’s just two people talking for an hour and a half. I would love to do something like that next. Is that what you’re looking to do going forward then? It could be anything. I really want to leave myself open. I would love to do something a little more scaled down, kind of dialogue-heavy thing. I could never have imagined the caliber of director and the caliber of actor that I’ve been working with. If I can only just continue to do that, I will be very lucky indeed. I’ve gotten to work with some of my absolute heroes, and that’s been wonderful. But I want to keep working in horror as well. Horror’s having a really exciting moment right now, especially young people in horror, with Obsession and Backrooms . I will stay as long as it’ll have me. Horror, fantasy — that’s what I grew up with, and I want to explore that more as well. What does your ideal day off look like? I would wake up at 10:30 a.m.-ish. I’m a very late-to-bed, late-to-rise kind of person in my free time. I’d wake up then; I’d get a coffee; I’d go for a walk. I have to do 10,000 steps a day. I’m like a dog. I have to be walked. Then I would go and see a movie. I would go to the cinema. I would probably go to the Prince Charles Cinema, which is my favorite in the world. I don’t know whether I’d see it on my own or with somebody else. I do go on my own to the cinema a lot. That’s one of my favorite ways to watch a film. Then I’d get a nice dinner. I might go shopping a little bit. I might go record shopping, go DVD shopping. Then I would go to the pub maybe, and then I would go to bed at 1 a.m. I’m being very specific with the times. I’m unfamiliar with Prince Charles Cinema; why is that your favorite theater? Just the vibe there, and the programming. There’s always something on there that’s worth seeing. I honestly have so much to thank that cinema for because the education in film that it has given me is just insane. I’ve seen so many films there for the first time. It’s one of the few places, in London especially, where you can see old films and cult films and things that don’t get screened very often. You can go and experience them in the theater, and that’s a very valuable thing. They were going to possibly get shut down, but they’ve just won the battle against the landlord or whatever. They’re going to be there for another 25 years. I’m very happy about that. THR

title: Netflix Edits Schizophrenia Scene Out Of Tyson Fury Doc After Wife Reveals Boxer Does Not Have Condition
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Netflix Edits Schizophrenia Scene Out Of Tyson Fury Doc After Wife Reveals Boxer Does Not Have Condition International Insider: Doha Days; Tricky Week For BAFTA; ‘Remarried Empress’ Interview Canal+ Sends Signal To African Creative Community With Academy Launch Backed By President Of South Africa View All November 27, 2026 6:56am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Tyson Fury' Netflix Tyson Fury does not have schizophrenia and a scene in which his wife claims he does has been edited out of the Netflix movie about the British boxing superstar. The doc, titled Tyson Fury, provides a tell-all account of Fury’s mental health struggles as he builds up to his fight with Anthony Joshua next month, which is also on Netflix. The trailer initially showed Fury’s wife Paris Fury saying the boxer is a “mild schizophrenic,” but amid questions from the boxing regulator, this has now been revealed to be untrue. Related Stories News Netflix Tunes Into Music-Driven Chinese Fantasy Series 'The Melody Of Love' News Netflix Posts Racy Thanksgiving Message On 'The Hunting Wives' Season 2 Premiere Day “I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary,” a statement from Paris Fury said. “I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson’s condition and I used the word ‘schizophrenic.’ While Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn’t have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.” Watch on Deadline A Netflix spokeswoman said the scene has been removed from the doc, which dropped today. “Following new information shared by the family relating to Tyson’s official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch,” she added. Following the schizophrenia comments, which were also included in a Netflix press release about the doc on Monday, the British Boxing Board of Control said it had been examining whether what was thought to be Fury’s diagnosis would get in the way of his long-anticipated fight with fellow British boxer Joshua. That fight has now been cleared to take place on December 11 in Cardiff and could prove to be one of Netflix’s most lucrative live sporting events. Fury’s doc is billed as a “raw, real, unfiltered” look at “the man behind the boxing icon.” Fury has also appeared in two seasons of Netflix’s ob-doc At Home With the Furys, with a third in motion. title: Wildling Pictures Acquires Screen Rights To WWII Spy Story ‘Operation Sparrow’ & Folk Horror Novel ‘Queen Mab’
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Denis Villeneuve “Deeply Disappointed” That ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Will Launch On Same Weekend As ‘Dune: Part Three’ Neil Patrick Harris & Patton Oswalt Get Behind iPhone-Shot Short ‘Dropping Off’ About LA Rideshare Driver Wildling Pictures Acquires Screen Rights To WWII Spy Story ‘Operation Sparrow’ & Folk Horror Novel ‘Queen Mab’ View All November 27, 2026 5:52am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Operation Sparrow, Queen Mab Wildling Pictures EXCLUSIVE : Toronto-based film and TV company Wildling Pictures has optioned Emily McBride’s psychological folk horror novel Queen Mab and Jason Bell’s WWII spy story Operation Sparrow , with a view to turning both into features. Published in September this year, Bell’s archival research uncovers a little known but significant espionage operation from WWII which helped protect the D-Day landings. Drawing on newly declassified OSS files, the spy thriller “tells the true story of three American officers who parachuted into Nazi-allied Hungary in 1944 on a mission designed to end in their capture. Led by former New York Giants player and advertising executive Colonel Florimond Duke, the team used their Gestapo interrogations to convince Hitler that the Allied invasion would come through the Balkans rather than Normandy, diverting 12 German divisions away from the real D-Day landing site.” Related Stories News Tommy Dorfman Set To Direct Film Adaptation Of Mariko Tamaki's Graphic Novel 'Laura Dean Keeps Breaking Up With Me' News Book On Canadian World War II Spy Winthrop Bell Being Developed As Feature Film; Wildling Pictures & 'See For Me's Adam Yorke Attached Operation Sparrow is Wildling’s second option of Jason Bell’s work following the optioning of his book Cracking the Nazi Code , which Wildling is developing with screenwriter Adam Yorke ( Phreaker, See For Me) . Watch on Deadline The production company has also acquired the rights to Canadian author Emily McBride’s debut novel Queen Mab, the psychological folk horror which was released this summer. Screenwriter and director Emily O’Quinn Code ( Fresh Meat Mom, Bush Skeleton ) is onboard to write the screenplay. The well-received novel “follows a young scholar of fairy lore, Madeleine, as she loses her grip on reality to postpartum psychosis and must outwit her own logic before it drives her to do what the folklore prescribes.” The deal was done by Hotchkiss Daily and Associates on behalf of Sandra Pareja at Massie McQuilkin & Altman Literary Agents. Both projects are grounded in European settings and stories. Queen Mab is rooted in British and Irish folklore, while Operation Sparrow is rooted in Hungary and wider Central Europe. Wildling is currently in early discussions with potential global co-production partners across the UK, Ireland and the rest of Europe to develop the films for the international market. Wildling’s slate of literary adaptations also includes coming-of-age romantic comedy Laura Dean Keeps Breaking Up with Me , based on Mariko Tamaki’s graphic novel and co-produced with MXN Entertainment and Good Girl. The film stars Ava Phillippe and Sam Morelos and is directed by Tommy Dorfman. Matt Code, producer and President of Wildling Pictures, said: “Both Queen Mab and Operation Sparrow have the potential to open up their worlds on screen. Emily McBride has created a psychologically rich story that draws on the depth of British and Irish folklore, while Jason brings a hidden chapter of WWII history to light. Identifying these rich and distinctive literary IPs is a central part of Wildling’s approach to developing projects with both creative ambition and international reach and they’re a key part of our literary slate expansion.” Recent original productions for Wildling include Young Werther (TIFF 2024, Special Presentations) and Paying for It (TIFF 2024, Platform), as well as the comedy Suze (Santa Barbara International Film Festival 2024) and the thriller See for Me (Tribeca 2021, released in over 25 territories). The company has just wrapped production on its latest feature Devour starring Tricia Helfer, and written and directed by Erica Orofino. title: Justin Timberlake Rolls Back the Years on Silly, Sexy and Sincere Appearance on ‘Tonight Show’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Abid Rahman Plus Icon Abid Rahman International Editor, Digital gentlemanabroad Follow Sign Up View All November 27, 2026 4:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jimmy Fallon and Justin Timberlake perform the "Sexy Butterball Hotline" sketch. Todd Owyoung/NBC A game Justin Timberlake gave a welcome reminder of his varied talents on The Tonight Show on Thursday night, variously dressing up as a “sexy” turkey, doing a spirited Scottish accent and of course dancing and singing like only he can. In what felt like a throwback to the innocence and goofiness of the Obama years, Timberlake was on top form, taking part in sketches, dance bits and sitting down for an interview to promote the 20th anniversary of his classic album FutureSex/LoveSounds and the four-part documentary series Timberlake that begins streaming on Apple TV on Dec. 11. Related Stories TV Justin Timberlake Documentary Trailer: "He's Not Who I Thought He Was" Music Justin Timberlake Teases New Music: "I've Been Chef-ing" With the Roots backing them up, Fallon opened the show with Timberlake for a song and dance number, with the duo going through The History of Party Songs. In a segment that is catnip for 90s kids, the tracks covered included Soul II Soul’s “Back to Life (However Do You Want Me),” Ini Kamoze’s “Here Comes the Hotstepper,” Mark Morrison’s “Return of the Mack,” Montell Jordan’s “This Is How We Do It,” Spice Girls “Wannabe,” Bell Biv DeVoe’s “Poison,” Timberlake’s own “Rock Your Body” and more. In the interview section, Timberlake opened up about the making of FutureSex/LoveSounds , reminding the audience that that his influences on the album included “Bowie, David Byrne, Talking Heads, Freddie Mercury, Queen, Billy Idol, James Brown, Eurythmics and INXS.” He said that on the song “SexyBack” he was channeling Bowie doing “Rebel Rebel” and he had to fight the recording company on the production. “They fought me on it. Well, I brought it in and it was like, ‘It’s too fast.’ I was like, ‘That’s why it’s gonna work.’ … [And they said], ‘You don’t sound like you, your signature falsetto.’ I was like, ‘That’s why it’s gonna work.'” On the infamous lyrics to “SexyBack”, Timberlake added, “That song does not make any sense. I’ve said this. It makes zero sense. But, it’s why it makes sense.” In a particularly poignant part of the interview, Timberlake discussed his love for and influence of the late D’Angelo, describing him as “my guy.” “D’Angelo, for me, he changed everything. You know, he was one of those artists… rest in peace. What a brilliant, brilliant, brilliant artist. But I remember when he came out, it just like everything changed. [He] was a once-in-a-generation artist.” On why he decided to take part in the Apple docuseries — which Fallon said tackled Timberlake’s career highpoints and personal low points — the Grammy-winner said that initially he “was really reluctant to do it” agreeing with Fallon that he was “sort of famously private.” His relationship with director Fisher Stevens softened his stance and that the doc he has “mustered up some courage to talk about some things that I’ve never talked about before, that, you know, things that even those that are closest to me don’t know.” Timberlake said he found the doc experience “cathartic” and he hoped it would help others to share their troubles. “Everybody’s going through something. And I think I’ve gone through a lot in the last five years that I feel like have made me a better human and a better father, a better husband, a better friend.” In the recent past, Timberlake has had a number of public incidents including being arrested for DWI in the Hamptons in June 2024 and revealing in July 2025 that he was diagnosed with Lyme disease . There was also the cheating rumors in 2019, and subsequent public ridicule, after the singer was caught holding hands with co-star Alisha Wainwright during the filming of Palmer . Timberlake had to issue a public apology about the Palmer incident on Instagram, calling it a “strong lapse in judgment.” One sketch that’s likely to get a lot of play on social media was “Sexy Butterball Hotline,” where Fallon (Rocky Drumstick) and Timberlake (Pecker Spatchcock) played two very sexy turkeys — “the dirtiest birds in the coop” no less — manning an after dark Thanksgiving helpline. A sample of some of the lines from Rocky and Pecker in this bit: “Who says the turkey can’t be the one who does the stuffing?” “Is it Black Friday? ‘Cause my clothes are 100% off.” “I can’t wait till you lay me down on the table right in front of Grandma.” Good clean fun. It wouldn’t be a complete Timberlake Tonight Show appearance without a “Camp Winnipesaukee” sketch. Fallon and Timberlake once more donned the retainers and wigs to relive their awkward teenage years and play the annoying campers trying to sing a popular song much to the annoyance of the camp counselor. On Thursday’s episode, the pair decided to take on The Proclaimers’ 1988 hit “I’m Gonna Be (500 Miles)” with Timberlake and Fallon’s attempt at Scottish brogue worthy of commendation but ultimately short of passable. Proving he’s still one of the greatest singers and dancers around, Timberlake rounded his appearance with two medleys of his greatest hits. In the first clip he performed a medley of “FutureSex / LoveSound,” “SexyBack,” “Summer Love” and “My Love.” In a second clip he performed “LoveStoned,” “Until the End of Time” and “What Goes Around…/ … Comes Around.” Justin Timberlake and Jimmy Fallon on ‘The Tonight Show.’ Todd Owyoung/NBC THR

Even me being 10 years older than them, I have significant, great, wonderful memories,” she continued. “They were babies. They probably don’t even remember half the stuff [we do]. title: Gerald R. Molen, Oscar-Winning Producer on ‘Schindler’s List,’ Dies at 91
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All November 26, 2026 12:47pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Gerald R. Molen Greg Doherty/Getty Images Gerald R. Molen, the Oscar-winning producer who teamed with Steven Spielberg on films including Schindler’s List , Jurassic Park and Minority Report , has died. He was 91. A longtime resident of Bigfork, Montana, Molen died Monday, his great-niece Rachel Lorraine Pullan announced . Molen first worked with Spielberg as a unit production manager on The Color Purple (1985), after which the filmmaker offered him his first producing gig, as an associate producer on *batteries not included (1987). Related Stories Music Andy Taylor, Duran Duran Guitarist, Dies at 65 Lifestyle Veruschka, Mesmerizing Supermodel of the 1960s and '70s, Dies at 87 After serving as a producer on the Spielberg-directed Hook (1991), Molen was named head of production at Spielberg’s Amblin Entertainment, where he shepherded such films as The Flintstones (1994), The Little Rascals (1994), Little Giants (1994), Casper (1995), Twister (1996) and the Spielberg-directed sequel The Lost World: Jurassic Park (1997). “It was the best job in Hollywood,” he said in a 2023 interview, “because any movie [Spielberg] directed I got to produce, and any movie the company did I got to oversee.” He shared the best picture Oscar for Schindler’s List (1993) with Spielberg and Branko Lustig. Molen’s producing credits outside of Spielberg and Amblin included the best picture winner Rain Man (1988), Days of Thunder (1990), The Other Side of Heaven (2001), Just Like Heaven (2005), The Meg (2018) and Meg 2: The Trench (2023). Gerald Robert Molen was born on Jan. 6, 1935, in Great Falls, Montana. He and his family moved to North Hollywood in 1947, and his parents, Gerald Sr. and Edith, built a cafe across the street from Republic Pictures in Studio City. “I got to make friends with the studio guards,” he said in 2014. “They used to take me on the studio lot and take me to a soundstage or the backlot where they were maybe shooting a Western and stuff me down behind a bale of hay or under a wagon. I got it in my blood.” After high school, Molen enlisted in the U.S. Marine Corps; after 10 months in the service, he landed a job as a truck driver hauling furniture at Republic in 1957. He moved to Universal in 1959, and on Psycho (1960), he doubled for Anthony Perkins as the driver of a car heading to the Bates Motel (director Alfred Hitchcock was in the back seat giving directions). Molen rose to head of transportation at the studio, and as a transportation coordinator/captain/supervisor, he worked on Escape to Witch Mountain (1975), Bound for Glory (1976), Coming Home (1978), Being There (1979), Ordinary People (1980) and Absence of Malice (1981). He graduated to unit production manager on such movies as The Postman Always Rings Twice (1981), Tootsie (1982), A Soldier’s Story (1984) and the Spielberg-helmed The Color Purple before embarking on his career as a producer. Molen also had cameos in films including Rain Man , Days of Thunder , Jurassic Park and two other Spielberg-directed features, Amistad (1997) and Catch Me If You Can (2002). He produced 2016: Obama’s America (2012) and Hillary’s America: The Secret History of the Democratic Party (2016), two documentaries written and directed by Dinesh D’Souza that were critical of Barack Obama and Hilary Clinton. He wrote about the Obama doc in an opinion piece for THR . In 2014, he sent a letter to 866 Christian and conservative leaders that accused Hollywood of “depravity” and causing “much damage to America.” “Throughout my years in Hollywood, I tried to live my life differently and be a part of projects that I would be proud to have my grandchildren watch,” he wrote. “It hasn’t been easy, but I’ve at least tried to stand against the tide of depravity that has too often flourished there.” Pat, his wife of nearly 70 years, died in January 2024 at age 86. THR
